title: Meaning, not wording
hookLine: settling disagreements about the letter versus the meaning

lines: HALF PAST, OR THIRTY MINUTES PAST?
THE SAME THING, TEN MESSAGES IN.
cards: Two friends are arguing in a group chat. One says the meeting is at half past. The other says no, thirty minutes past.
Ten messages in, someone points out they're saying the same thing. Real disagreements are rarely that silly, but some turn out to be about the words, not the thing.
In a grove near the town of Kusinārā, the Buddha gives the monks a short talk on exactly this: what to do when the community disagrees about the teaching itself.

teach.b: He starts by reminding them what he's taught: the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the factors of awakening, the noble path. Train in these in harmony, he says, without quarreling. Then he's realistic.
Disputes will happen, so he sorts them.
Pali has two words here: attha, the meaning, and byañjana, the wording, literally the letters. Suppose two monks differ about both the meaning and the wording.
Then someone should go to the more approachable one and say gently: you differ about the meaning and the wording; please don't fall into a quarrel. Then the same with the other.

teach.h: SAME MEANING, DIFFERENT WORDS: A TRIFLE.
teach.b: If they differ about the meaning but agree on the wording, same approach: point it out, and keep the peace. But if they agree about the meaning and differ only about the wording, the Buddha says, the wording is a trifle.
Don't fall into a quarrel over a trifle. That's the heart of it. When people share what something means, the exact words are small.
The sutta then turns to correcting someone who has done wrong: don't rush; think first whether it will help, whether the person will listen, whether you can do it without distress.
If it can be done kindly, do it. On an ordinary day, this saves a lot of grief. Before arguing, ask: do we disagree about what this means, or only about how to say it?

how: Buddhist communities across the world chant and study the teachings in many languages and translations, and some teachers point to this sutta to explain why the meaning matters more than identical wording.

o: the exact letters a teaching is written in
the reward a teaching promises to you
attha: what a teaching is actually saying

games.q: meaning and wording: tap the pairs.
p: don't rush; ask if it will help

s: the Buddha says disputes over wording are the most serious
if the meaning is shared, he calls the wording a trifle.
the advice is to approach the more approachable of the two monks first
and to point out the difference gently, so it doesn't become a quarrel.
this talk was given near Kusinārā
in a grove near the town, where the monks were staying with him.

games.q: two monks agree on what a teaching means, but argue over which words to use for it. what does the Buddha say?
o: the wording is a trifle; don't quarrel over it
the one with the older wording is right
games.why: when the meaning is shared, the wording is a trifle. the Buddha tells the monks not to fall into a quarrel over a trifle.

practice: Bring to mind a recent disagreement, at home, at work or online, and replay it slowly. Ask what the other person meant, what you meant, and whether those were really different or you were fighting over a word.
If the meanings were close, picture saying so, I think we mean the same thing, and let your shoulders drop.

wordCard.voice: Meaning. Attha, what a teaching means, set beside byañjana, the wording. When the meaning is shared, the Buddha calls the wording a trifle.

orig.note: Pali attha (Sanskrit artha): meaning, purpose, benefit. set beside byañjana, the letter.

carryVoice: Your line: don't quarrel over a trifle. When the meaning is shared, the words are small. See you tomorrow.
